pooled-sampling.play: Pool the union of candidate outputs/systems and judge that pool, so no source is structurally favored.
pooled-sampling.does: Instead of judging the whole space, judge only the UNION of what the candidate systems produced/retrieved, then reuse those judgments to score all systems — including ones absent from the pool.
pooled-sampling.cost: Pooling BIAS — systems that surface relevant items OUTSIDE the pool are underrated (a sampling_frame cost).
pooled-sampling.modality_notes: Canonical in IR (judge top-k of each run, reuse qrels); generalizes to model-comparison eval (judge the union of outputs the candidate models produced, reuse the rubric across them). 'Don't judge the whole space' is invariant.

control-attestation.name: Control Attestation (No Assumed Controls)
control-attestation.play: Every convention-required control names an owner and attaches evidence it ran; 'assumed handled upstream' is not an allowed status — an unattested control is treated as absent and audited.
control-attestation.does: Require each convention-mandated control to be explicitly attested at execution — owner, version, and evidence it was applied — so a control can't be silently reclassified as an out-of-scope assumption. Anything marked 'assumed' or unattested is scoped INTO the audit, not out of it, closing the gap where the primary control and its only catch layer disappear together.
control-attestation.cost: Attestation overhead per control + the discipline to audit the assumptions; surfaces work that was previously (wrongly) counted as done.
control-attestation.modality_notes: Invariant across modalities — the control list is workflow-specific, but 'an assumed control is an unaudited control' holds everywhere. This is the datasheet discipline applied to the audit strategy itself: make the assumed-handled steps explicit so they become checkable rather than presumed.

partial-input-baseline.name: Partial-Input Baseline (Leakage Diagnostic)
partial-input-baseline.play: Try to predict the label from a fragment of the input; if you can, the label is leaking a proxy.
partial-input-baseline.does: Score a baseline that sees only PART of the input — the hypothesis alone, the answer without the question, the caption without the image. If it beats chance, the label is derivable from a fragment that shouldn't suffice: the data has an artifact a model will exploit instead of the intended signal.
partial-input-baseline.cost: Cheap to run, but only DETECTS leakage — removing it needs re-collection (adversarial / model-in-the-loop) or reweighting.
partial-input-baseline.modality_notes: The 'fragment' is modality-specific — hypothesis-only (NLI), answer-only (multiple-choice QA), caption-without-image (vision-language), first-N-tokens (sequence) — but 'predict the label from a part that shouldn't be enough' is invariant. It is a diagnostic, not a fix.

construct-validity.name: Construct Validity
construct-validity.tenet: The label must measure the construct you actually intend, not a proxy that merely correlates with it. "Good" data is data where the thing you operationalize and the thing you care about are the same thing — not data where the model can hit the target by reading a shortcut.
construct-validity.probe: Can the label be predicted from a fragment of the input, or from a spurious cue (length, format, source, fluency)? If a partial-input baseline beats chance, you are measuring the proxy.

evidence.claim: A hypothesis-only model reaches ~67% on SNLI (vs 33% chance) — the crowd writing protocol left label-predictive artifacts, so models "pass" by exploiting the proxy, not by inferring.
evidence.source: Gururangan et al., Annotation Artifacts in NLI Data (NAACL 2018); Poliak et al., Hypothesis-Only Baselines (2018)

evidence.claim: Measurement modeling — making the construct → operationalization mapping explicit — is what exposes where a label and its intended construct silently diverge.

internal-validity.name: Internal Validity (Freedom from Confounds)
internal-validity.tenet: No spurious cue may ride along with the signal. If something other than the construct — order, author, tier, background texture — covaries with the label, the model learns the shortcut and the data is good only on the distribution where that correlation happens to hold.
internal-validity.probe: List every cue that correlates with the label but isn't the construct. Hold each fixed (or randomize it) and check the judgment survives. Does presentation order leak into the label?

evidence.claim: Models reliably latch onto "shortcut" features (texture, backgrounds, artifacts) that predict the label in-distribution but aren't the intended construct — and fail off it.
evidence.source: Geirhos et al., Shortcut Learning in Deep Neural Networks (Nature MI 2020)

evidence.claim: Datasets carry a measurable built-in bias: a classifier can name the source dataset of an image, proving spurious source-cues are baked into supposedly neutral labels.
evidence.source: Torralba & Efros, Unbiased Look at Dataset Bias (CVPR 2011)

reliability.name: Reliability (Reproducible Judgments)
reliability.tenet: Two competent annotators given the same item and guideline must reach the same label at a rate well above chance. Low inter-annotator agreement means "good" isn't yet defined — the construct lives in individual heads, not in the protocol. Reliability is the precondition for validity.
reliability.probe: Put two raters on the same items and compute a chance-corrected agreement (Cohen's κ / Krippendorff's α). Below the field's threshold, iterate the guideline on the disagreements before scaling — don't average your way past an undefined construct.

evidence.claim: Chance-corrected agreement (and its thresholds) is the standard instrument for whether a coding scheme is reliable enough to trust; raw percent-agreement overstates it.
evidence.source: Krippendorff, Content Analysis (2004); Artstein & Poesio, Inter-Coder Agreement for CL (Comp. Ling. 2008)

evidence.claim: Modeling each annotator's confusion matrix (EM) recovers a better gold label from noisy, disagreeing labelers than majority vote — reliability can be estimated, not just assumed.
evidence.source: Dawid & Skene, Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Observer Error-Rates (JRSS-C 1979)

external-validity.name: External Validity (Representativeness)
external-validity.tenet: The labeled sample must mirror the deployment distribution, including the rare-but-important tail. Data that is "good" only on the easy, over-sampled cases is not good where the model will actually run. The sampling frame is part of the definition of good, not a downstream detail.
external-validity.probe: Is your labeled set a stratified mirror of deployment, or whatever was cheapest to collect? Are the rare classes represented enough to learn — and audited across the full distribution, not a convenience sample?

evidence.claim: Severe natural class imbalance (~1:10k) plus a geographically narrow collection frame (two cities) bounds what the resulting labels can certify about real deployment.
Documenting the population, sampling process, and what's NOT covered is how a dataset's external validity becomes auditable instead of assumed.
evidence.source: Gebru et al., Datasheets for Datasets (CACM 2021)

ground-truth-anchoring.name: Ground-Truth Anchoring
ground-truth-anchoring.tenet: A validated gold reference must exist to check labels against — and the gold itself must be audited, because the gold standard is the thing most likely to be quietly wrong. Without an anchor, "good" collapses into "whatever the producer emitted with confidence."
ground-truth-anchoring.probe: What is your ground truth, and who validated IT? If a model defines or judges good, is it perceiving quality or recalling its own family's style — would a different model family agree?

evidence.claim: Even canonical test sets carry pervasive label errors (~3.4% across 10 benchmarks); the gold you trust as the anchor is itself a measurement that needs auditing.
evidence.source: Northcutt et al., Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets (NeurIPS 2021)

evidence.claim: LLM judges show position, verbosity, and self-enhancement bias — a model anchor can score its own family's outputs higher, so the anchor must be cross-checked across families.
evidence.source: Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge / MT-Bench & Chatbot Arena (NeurIPS 2023)

contamination-control.name: Contamination Control (Train/Eval Isolation)
contamination-control.tenet: The evaluation signal is only good if the answer wasn't already seen in training. Leakage between train and eval — or the answer being derivable from a feature absent at deployment — makes "good" performance an artifact of memorization rather than capability.
contamination-control.probe: Could any eval item (or a near-duplicate) appear in training? Is the solution visible in the prompt? Decontaminate by entity/time partition and re-measure — the gap is your real signal.

evidence.claim: Filtering solution-leakage and pre-cutoff contamination from a code benchmark dropped measured resolution roughly threefold — uncontrolled leakage inflated "good" by ~3x.
evidence.source: Aleithan et al., SWE-Bench+ (2024); Jimenez et al., SWE-Bench (ICLR 2024)

statistical-power.name: Statistical Power (Sufficient Evidence)
statistical-power.tenet: Enough items (and an appropriate test design) that, if a real effect exists, the experiment detects it as significant rather than dismissing it as noise. An underpowered split can't distinguish a real difference from chance, so a "good" result may be noise and may not replicate.
statistical-power.probe: For the smallest effect you care about, what is the probability your test set would yield a significant result — is it sized to reach the conventional 80% power, or are you reading noise?

evidence.claim: Typical machine-translation test sets of 2000 sentences have only ~75% power to detect a 1 BLEU-point difference; for several GLUE tasks the small test sets leave most comparisons to state-of-the-art underpowered, so a real improvement is easily mistaken for noise.
evidence.source: Card et al., With Little Power Comes Great Responsibility (EMNLP 2020)

evidence.claim: Typical human-rating study designs are also underpowered to detect the small model differences that are frequently studied.
evidence.source: Card et al., With Little Power Comes Great Responsibility (EMNLP 2020)

incentive-alignment.name: Incentive Alignment (Goodhart-Resistance)
incentive-alignment.tenet: Annotators must not be able to reach 'good' by optimizing the pay/quota structure (templating, speed-clicking) instead of producing quality. When the measure becomes the target, it stops measuring.
incentive-alignment.probe: How are annotators paid, and can they maximize earnings without producing quality? Seed honeypots / fraud checks and measure how much of your data survives them.

evidence.claim: Across 38 MTurk studies, a large share of respondents fraudulently accessed studies via virtual private servers; these fraudulent respondents produced particularly low-quality data that weakened treatment effects — and the fraud increased over time as workers adapted to the incentive, so static checks become an arms race.
evidence.source: Kennedy et al., The Shape of and Solutions to the MTurk Quality Crisis (PSRM 8(4), 2020)

construct-stability.name: Construct Stability (No Drift / Inflation)
construct-stability.tenet: The bar for 'good' must hold fixed across the campaign — neither creeping upward (leniency inflation) nor shifting under you as the data/model changes. A moving definition makes early and late labels incomparable.
construct-stability.probe: Re-score frozen anchor exemplars across the campaign — does the standard drift? Is the guideline frozen before scoring, and do you measure intra-annotator agreement over time?

evidence.claim: Intra-annotator agreement is not stable: re-labeling the same items after a delay, word- alignment consistency degraded steadily across 1-week / 2-week / 1-month intervals, and rating consistency fell as the re-test interval grew — so the same annotator drifts against their own earlier judgments unless anchored.
evidence.source: Li et al. (word-alignment, 2010); Kiritchenko & Mohammad (best-worst rating reliability, 2017)

provenance-documentation.name: Provenance & Documentation
provenance-documentation.tenet: The origin, collection process, and labeling decisions must be recorded, so the data's fitness can be audited rather than assumed. Documentation is the cross-cutting precondition that makes every other principle checkable after the fact.
provenance-documentation.probe: Could a downstream user reconstruct who labeled what, under which guideline version, sampled from where — and is every convention-required control attested rather than assumed?

evidence.claim: A datasheet of 57 questions across 7 categories (motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing/labeling, uses, distribution, maintenance) — by analogy to the electronics datasheets that accompany every component — makes a dataset's fitness auditable by its consumers instead of assumed.
evidence.source: Gebru et al., Datasheets for Datasets (CACM 64(12), 2021); Bender & Friedman, Data Statements for NLP (TACL 2018)
